Since the glow source sits behind and below the zombie, the rim should appear as a thin bright line concentrated along the top edges and shoulders where backlighting would naturally catch, not evenly around the whole silhouette.

I should try a different approach: use a thin pointed round brush with varied pressure to paint gesture strokes only along selected edges facing the flash — the face profile, top surfaces of the arms, and front of the chest. The shirt color looks good already. I'm debating whether to retry this on the wet scratch or set up a fresh trial area, but since this thin-brush technique already worked well on the cowboy's lit face edge, I just need to place the rim precisely just inside the silhouette boundary.

I'll trace along the zombie's contour points, offsetting the strokes inward by about one to one and a half units, focusing the warm orange flash-lit rim on the left-facing edges (head profile, arm fronts, chest edge, front leg, hands) and a fainter pale-yellow sky rim on the back-facing edges like the hump and coat tail. Clipping the strokes to the zombie's mask should let the bristles stop cleanly at the silhouette, giving a crisp edge with just the inner half of the stroke visible.

Working out lit top edges for the lower arm and torso contours, then moving to the front leg ribbon coordinates, factoring in the flash's angle from upper-left to determine which edges catch light.

I'm also mapping the back edges — hump, tail, and back leg — for a thinner, sparser pale gold rim-light pile separate from the warm front flash highlights, and now starting to think through the zombie's overall silhouette construction.

The flat dark form needs rim and flash lighting to give it shape, plus a flash-lit plane on the chest. I want to strengthen the blood spatter impact with a few larger dark-red drops and bigger flying chunks, but first I'll darken the shirt and add the rim lighting in the painting.

events.text:
The shirt came out brighter yellow-olive rather than the darker mustard I expected — odd given the raw umber, ochre, green earth, white and black mix should read as dark olive. I'm wondering if the detail hand coverage isn't fully obscuring the lighter shirt underneath.

Also looking at the rim lines along the arms and legs — they read as uniform cartoon-ish outlines, acceptable for a backlit figure but could use more variation and softness in places. And there's a concerning pinkish-white streaking near the head where I covered old gore marks, which reads unintentionally like feathers or a halo rather than sky — I need to better match it to the surrounding gold-peach tones. The dark red gore mark at the back of the head looks right but small, so I want to zoom into that area to check it more carefully.

I'm looking at the pinkish streaks from the peach patches and considering repainting them with a better-matched sky color rather than trying to disguise them as intentional elements. Since I can't directly sample pixel colors, I'll need to estimate the surrounding peach/gold tones near that area and test a patch before committing.

Working through the distance calculation at (850,300), I find the point sits between the gold and apricot sky zones, roughly 22% gold and 78% apricot. I'm now figuring out how to re-knife a matched color pile by blending the apricot recipe (white, orange chrome, vermilion, ochre) at that ratio with the gold recipe, while accounting for the palette's 16-pile limit and whether the original piles have been scraped.

Since I'll need to cover the streak zone anyway, I realize I can lay a tiny trial dab of the mixed color right in that area without risk — it's harmless because that section needs recovering regardless. But I'm also considering whether the existing sky layer underneath has set or is still wet, since the peach streak was laid four days ago and might now be dry enough that painting over it behaves differently than working wet-into-wet.

I'll let that section dry more and move on to other elements first — the shirt and the spray effects. For the gore spray, I want to make it bigger and more dramatic, a heavier plume of dark-red mist with some chunks rather than fine dots. For the shirt, I'm thinking of mixing a darker olive-umber tone (raw umber, green earth, bone black, ochre, a touch of lead white) to replace the mustard color, and making the stripe narrower and broken up so it reads as a torn shirt rather than a solid band — possibly dropping the stripe motif entirely.

I'm now reconsidering whether to repaint directly into the open paint, which might muddy it toward a dark olive-brown that could actually look right, but it's unpredictable. Since time isn't a constraint here, I'll just wait several days for it to dry properly before touching it again.

The color match checks out across the streak zone's sky tones, so I'll go ahead and repaint that ribbon-like streak region using the sky match color.

Darkening the foreground land and adding a cast shadow plus a cool rim light on his back edge (against the blue-violet sky) should help separate him, especially since the glow behind the zombie lights his front warmly while his back stays in shadow. The muzzle flash reads fine, and the zombie silhouette is working, though the shirt still feels too flat.

Now I'm thinking the legs need more modeling — a lit front edge on the forward leg instead of flat grey-blue strips. The foreground also feels empty, so I want to add long, soft shadows cast from the zombie and the crosses toward the viewer, since the low horizon glow would stretch shadows dramatically across the ground and help unify the composition — figuring out the exact direction based on where the glow sits relative to the figures.

Now I want to fix the zombie's head so it reads less like a round ball — deepen the base tone, sink the eye and cheekbone, and keep a flash-lit edge only on the face front. There's currently a stray light ring on the left side that's reading as a helmet rather than a zombie feature, so I'll repaint over that with the dark skin base before adding the lit highlights back in.
The crop is too small at this scale—2.4px/unit means a 65-unit crop only gives me 156px. Since I can't upscale, I should try adjusting the size parameter alongside the crop instead.

The head reads as a gray-olive egg shape with a dark eye and open mouth, lit along the profile edge, but the wound on the back feels too subtle. I'm thinking I should darken the head overall since it's too light grayish, and add a stronger dark burst at the wound exit point for more impact.

I'll glaze the back half of the head darker with skin tone and bone black, keeping the front third lit, then add accent details like a brow ridge. Next I want to tackle cast shadows for the whole scene: with the sun low on the horizon, the zombie's shadow would stretch as a long dark band from its feet down toward the viewer, splaying slightly where the legs separate, so I'm working out the direction and width of that shadow based on the sun's position relative to the feet.

For the crosses, I'm calculating their shadow direction too, pointing left-down away from the sun, drawing them as thin dark lines extending a couple times the cross height with a small crossbar blob — these long shadows pointing toward the cowboy should read as striking graphic elements.

Now considering the cowboy: his feet sit low in frame, so his shadow would cast toward the lower-left and exit the canvas quickly given his proximity to the bottom edge. I'm also questioning whether the lighting even supports long shadows here — with the sun sitting right at the horizon, the ground is barely lit and realistically wouldn't show strong shadows, but for the image's impact I'll let the shadows read dramatically anyway.

Another idea is to use the muzzle flash itself as a light source — casting the zombie's shadow away from the cowboy and pooling warm light on the ground beneath the gun, which would tie the flash to the space and light the zombie's front. I don't want to overdo it with too many competing light effects, so I'll prioritize the long cool shadows from the horizon glow first.

For those shadows, I'll test a cool dark glaze (ultramarine, raw umber, bone black, rose madder at low opacity) applied with long brush strokes, clipped to the shadow mask so it doesn't spill past the land shapes. I'll also add a subtle vignette darkening the foreground to frame the scene. Let me try a quick test swatch on scratch space first to see how the glaze sits over the dry land base.

I'll plan the rag width relative to each shadow's thickness and do three passes, refolding and redipping the rag between wipes.

local function dir(bx, by) local dx, dy = bx - S[1], by - S[2] local n = math.sqrt(dx*dx + dy*dy) return dx/n, dy/n end
local r = rag{width=16}
local function lift(pts, passes)
  for p = 1, passes do
    r:refold() r:dip(1.0)
    r:wipe(pts, {pressure=1.0})
  end
end
for i, c in ipairs(crosses_def) do
  local bx, by, h = c[1], c[2], c[3]
  local ux, uy = dir(bx, by)
  local L = 1.3 * h * (0.6 + 0.4*smoothstep(500, 620, by))
  local s0 = 6
  lift({{bx + ux*s0, by + uy*s0}, {bx + ux*(L+6), by + uy*(L+6)}}, 3)
  local cx, cy = bx + ux*L*0.74, by + uy*L*0.74
  local bl = h*0.27
  lift({{cx - bl - 6, cy + 1}, {cx + bl + 6, cy - 1}}, 3)
end
-- zombie leg shadows

The repaint cleared the scrub too, but that's fine since it was spotty, and the ground reads clean now. Looking at the overall scene, it's working: cowboy shooting, zombie hit. The cowboy's reddish-brown coat reads as a mid-value mass—not quite the dark silhouette I imagined, but acceptable as is.

Going through remaining issues: the zombie's shirt is still too saturated ochre-yellow and needs checking against the darker zb_shirt2 I painted. The muzzle flash and smoke puff read fine, gore spray works as a red mist though I could emphasize the hit more. The ground feels a bit empty and would benefit from sparse scrub silhouettes, foreground stones, and contact shadows under both characters' feet to ground them properly.

Looking at the overall composition now, the sky and cowboy's profile face read well, but the coat-to-ground value contrast in the lower half is too weak—the red-brown coat and mauve-brown ground are too similar in value and need more separation. I'm also considering intensifying the drama with a bigger warm glow halo around the muzzle flash lighting the cowboy's arm/sleeve, and making the zombie read more ghoulish with greener skin tones.

I'm noticing the lower halves of the figures blend into the ground since the ground value is close to the coat's darkness, which actually matches how twilight silhouettes naturally lose definition near the feet rather than being an error to fix.

One fix is lightening the mid-ground band (around y 480-600) with a mauve tone reflecting the sky, so the zombie's legs and the cowboy's coat hem read more clearly without disturbing the darker foreground. I'm also considering making the cowboy's coat darker overall for a near-silhouette effect, which would still read as distinct against the mid-dark ground.

Since he faces the glow on the right, his front side should be warmly lit while his back (left, facing the dark eastern sky) should be glazed darker for volume — that contrast would also help the coat's hem stand out more against the mid-dark mauve ground instead of looking flat and uniform. Next I want to check how the zombie's shirt is reading.

The zombie shirt still reads olive-yellow with a stripe shaped like a long leaf, and the body is a flat dark purple-gray with a rounded hunchback silhouette that works fine for a zombie. The head looks bald now that the hair streaks are gone, with some red gore at the back.

The entry wound checks out logically — bullet hits the face from the left and sprays out the back right — but overall the zombie still reads as a flat cutout with just rim lighting. I'm considering adding mid-tone modeling on the coat folds, lighter patches of rotting cloth, and green-gray tones on the hands and face, though at this scale such detail might be too fine to matter. The bigger priority is making sure the blast stays the clear focal point, possibly strengthening the glow on the cowboy's hand, the gun's underside, and the sleeve, while also giving the zombie being hit more visual weight.

The red mist from the impact needs to read as a denser, chunkier burst rather than diffuse red dust — I want to thicken it near the head with larger drops and reinforce the exit wound, since repainting the sky patch behind the head stripped some of it away. Beyond that, I'm noting remaining fixes: coat modeling with a darker back half on the cowboy, contact shadows and scattered stones at the feet, confirming the old shadow outlines are fully covered, and maybe adding a single bright evening star near the glow in the upper sky as a nice finishing touch.

The mesas as flat violet silhouettes look solid already, though a subtle lit top edge could help — otherwise they're fine as is. Now I want to focus on the cowboy's gun hand area.

I'm checking the muzzle flash details — the tiny gun, the cylinder-gap jets, the pale halo with white core and orange tongues, and the gray-white smoke cloud reading as billowing black powder smoke, though the flash direction seems off toward the upper right.

The zombie's head wound needs work too — the spray of dark red droplets is detached from the head, with a gap that breaks the connection, so I want to add a denser, attached burst with chunks fanning from the back of the skull. Otherwise the hat, sky clouds, land texture, crosses, and mesa all feel solid, and the overall value structure is working.

The flash deserves the most attention since it's the focal point — the tongues read as separated hard-edged rays rather than a unified ball of fire with a bright core and a few spikes, and the muzzle smoke could use more warmth from internal light. I'm considering a thin translucent orange glaze over the tongues (avoiding the white core) to unify them into a glowing mass, or alternatively adding a few more fluid curving flame strokes to blend the separate tongues together.

The muzzle flash looks a bit cartoonish with weak white core and carroty orange tongues, and there's a gap between the gun muzzle around x=490 and where the flash core starts around x=507 that I need to close up.

To fix: I'll blot in a brighter, thicker white core right at the muzzle exit, soften the flash tongues so they feel more like burning gas rather than uniform carrot shapes with some thin yellow-white streaks inside, and give the smoke more volume with a darker underside against the lighter top.

Stepping back to review the whole piece: the cowboy silhouette and zombie with its orange rim lighting work well, but the "blasting" impact isn't convincing since the zombie's head doesn't look hit — the red gore spray is too diffuse and positioned too far from the head to read as a direct hit.

I'm reworking the gore effect so it reads as a concentrated burst right behind the skull rather than a vague cloud: starting with a small dense cluster of dark red just behind the head, then fanning spatter outward and upward, denser near the point of impact and sparser further out, since the bullet trajectory from the muzzle aligns correctly with the head height. The rest of the composition — cowboy left, flash center, zombie right, scattered crosses against the dominant sky and flat violet mesas — reads fine as is.

Looking over remaining fixes: the flash needs to pop more since the sky glow is nearly as bright as the core, so I'll make the white core bigger and purer rather than dimming the sky. The zombie's clawed hands and silhouette already read well, and the cowboy's profile is solid, but the hat brim highlight stroke looks a bit off and may need softening.

I'm also reconsidering the coat's wavy hem (slightly cartoonish but acceptable), the crosses (clean with good rim lighting), and the grave hole with its dirt heap, which reads fine as-is. I'm planning to thicken the white core into a teardrop shape stretching from the muzzle tip outward, add thinner white jets along the flame tongues, then layer in yellow between the core and the orange tongues for a smoother transition, leaving the orange tongues themselves untouched. The lilac smoke's shading seems fine without further adjustment, so I'll move straight into painting the core.

The muzzle now has a white-hot core, a cream blend of lead white and lemon chrome, with thin yellow streaks — a bit blobby but it reads as a gunshot blast. Next I'm checking the paint state at the zombie head's gore burst, since that layer was laid down on day 62 and it's now day 85, so it's likely dry.

I'm spotting artifacts from the image blending process—a straight diagonal line across the sky suggesting a hard edge from one blend mask, plus a curved edge in the top-right tile that looks like another mask boundary.

Moving through the figures, the hat's crown rim is too stark and bright, almost a white stripe, though the face and profile lighting look fine. The coat's scratchy white specks read as acceptable cloth texture, but the boots have a ghostly light halo around them that needs another darker patch pass. The zombie's olive shirt stripe reads oddly like a sash but is passable as a dirty open coat, while its feet are still just plain blob shapes that need more definition.

I'm now looking at the grave hole, which reads too flat and graphic like a manhole — it should instead look like disturbed dirt with an irregular mound and lit rim, rather than a clean black ellipse. The distant tombstone bump and the cross highlights both read fine, and the far land's horizontal brush banding looks acceptable too.

The mound piles and the flash's halo with its lavender-gray smoke cloud both work. The main problem now is the sky — there are hard straight edges and a curved line left over from the blend masks that need smoothing, plus a hard horizontal boundary between the rose and apricot sky tones that needs softening.

There's another hard edge visible around y≈190 in the left tile spanning x 0-700px, confirming these mask boundaries are creating visible seams across the sky. The fix is to paint over these seams with interlocking strokes of the neighboring sky colors directly over the dry paint, essentially repainting the whole upper sky band with a fresh pass using the same graded color piles plus some cloud strokes to disguise the transitions.

Actually I realize blending with a mask inherently creates a seam at the mask boundary itself, so using softer edges might grade it better, or I could skip blending entirely and rely on wet-into-wet strokes. My plan is to repaint the upper sky region above y=270 (excluding the figures) with a full-coverage sky color pass to restore a smooth gradient, then add cloud bands with gestural strokes painted wet-into-wet so they blend naturally without any hard mask edges.

But I realize the repaint boundary at y=270 would itself create a new seam unless I match colors carefully and use a "lost" edge to feather it, since the original sky passes below that line were already blended with cloud bands.

Stepping back, looking at the whole image, that straight diagonal band actually reads as a somewhat artificial cloud edge, so it's worth fixing given the sky covers 60% of the picture. I'm planning the repaint region as the sky mask above roughly y=285, excluding the cowboy's hat area with some growth margin.

Now I need to also exclude the smoke/flash region, since the smoke top extends up to around y=260 rather than 290, and account for the zombie's gore spray which reaches as high as y≈225 near x 840-900. So the cleanest boundary is a curve that sits around y=270 for most of the width but rises to y=215 near x>850 to clear the gore droplets.

There's also a seam near y≈240 where the m3 tile's lower edge runs diagonally from about y=225 at x=1000 to y=250 at x=400, overlapping the gore droplets region (x 850-950, y 225-330) — rather than solving this with one global mask, I think it's better to fix seams locally by painting short interlocking strokes blending the two color regions, so let me crop and look closely at the upper-left seams first.

The cloud bank's smooth arc top and straight horizontal bottom look too artificial, like a lenticular shape rather than a natural cloud. I want to break up those clean edges by adding cloud strokes that cross over them, blending in colors from the surrounding sky.

I'm noting the sky colors at each zone—deep dusk violet above the bank, lighter mauve-pink within it, periwinkle below—and planning to break each edge with interlocking horizontal strokes of the adjacent colors rather than a clean line. Before committing on the main painting, I want to run a quick scratch trial: paint a hard two-tone seam, let it dry, then test whether the softened-mask blend actually smooths it without introducing new artifacts.

Checking other elements: the spark trail from the bullet works, the blood spray behind the zombie is decent, the cowboy's coat and hem edge read cleanly, and the crosses/grave mounds are cartoonish but acceptable. The main weakness I'm spotting is the empty foreground and the lack of contact shadows under both the cowboy's and zombie's feet, making them look like they're floating — I want to add soft shadows there. The sky and distant mesa shapes are working well, and overall the figures read dark against the light sky in a squint test, so now I'm focusing on whether the blast effect itself needs more emphasis.

Thinking about the gore more — the spatter direction is fine as is, and a moderate burst feels right rather than overdoing it; a ground glow from the muzzle flash isn't really necessary. The bigger gap is that the cowboy's silhouette lacks a warm rim light along the side facing the glow, since I painted over that earlier rim treatment with the coat repaint — I should add a thin warm rim along his hat brim, face, arm, coat edge, and leg to match the light direction.

The mesas and sky look solid, the bottom shading is good and dark now, and there's a tiny stray dark dot on the left land that's probably just a scrub mark, not a concern. The head reads as a flat brownish blob rather than a believable profile, and the hat's highlights look like glossy plastic streaks instead of dull felt — I want to tone those down and make the crown's shine more subtle.

The profile shows warm light along the nose, lips, and chin from the sunset glow at lower right, while under the brim stays in shadow, which checks out. The hat feels oversized for the head but reads as cowboy-style so it's acceptable, though I'm still thinking about whether the proportions and face flatness need more adjustment.

There's no visible hair, just a dark area behind the ear, and the sleeve reads as a flat silhouette band that could use more form but works overall. Looking at priorities, the flash effect is the weakest link — it reads a bit cartoonish with its pale yellow halo and sharp flame tongues, so I'm considering brightening the core and blending the flame edges into the surrounding glow to make it feel more painterly and less like a sprite.

The flash looks decent and the smoke, while a bit cumulus-cartoony, is acceptable—maybe I'll add a few drifting, more transparent wisps. Reviewing the overall scene now, I'm checking the cowboy's head, hat, bandana, and shoulder mass for any remaining issues.

The zombie reads well overall, though more distinct flash light on the face could help, and the gore burst works. The crosses and land are fine, mesas read as flat violet shapes, and the open grave hole at the zombie's feet makes sense as the hole he crawled from — maybe add a dirt mound, though there's already one at the right. The claw-like hands work, and while the cowboy's gun arm shoulder lacks real anatomy, it still reads fine, with his stepping legs looking good.

For final touches I'm thinking about adding a signature in the bottom-right corner, a few dark wisps or sparks, and possibly a faint warm flash light on the ground, though that last one may not be necessary. Let me take one more close look at the zombie in its current state.

The zombie reads well now with its hunched posture, claws, gore burst, and decayed gray-green skull with yellowish streaks. I'm also noticing a tiny dark mark near the horizon that might be a small tombstone shape I'd spotted earlier.

events.text:
## Handoff — end of sitting (day 149)
State: finished and signed ("Claude", rigger, red earth/white/umber medium .2, bottom right, over dry ground). Title: "Boot Hill, Last Light".
Unresolved / could be taken further:
- Land plain is smooth and plain (deliberate after 3 failed texture trials, see above); a future try could be a very thin dark glaze graded toward the bottom edge only.
- Coat is one smooth red-brown mass with soft folds and a hairline rim; it could take a few more fold accents, laid over DRY paint with no blender.
- Muzzle smoke is a cartoon cumulus puff; a thin wisp trailing back over the arm might soften it.
- Gore burst at the zombie's head reads as a red rosette plus a spray. Acceptable, but stylised.
- A tiny dark mark on the horizon at about (772,470), left from early work; it reads as a distant headstone, so I left it.
Practical lessons (marked hypotheses where only seen once or twice):
1. Light accents laid into OPEN dark paint vanish (seen 4x: hand, face, coat bands, flash core). Let the dark set (dry/tacky) first. Fairly solid.
2. blend() over a figure after a light passage on part of it spreads the light everywhere (3x). For rim light, use a single pointed round line along a traced edge (scan mask:at to get the edge polyline), and no blender.
3. Rag lift with dip 1.0, pressure 1, refold each pass, 3+ passes: clears a thin wet glaze but leaves an outline ghost at the rim; plan to overpaint after it sets. Knife scrape barely lifts thin glaze.
4. A darkening glaze that works: transparent darks + medium .75-.8, hand=glaze, coverage 2, fill=true, then blend inside the same mask. Without blend it is blotchy; thinner instead of medium gives grainy specks.
5. Hold-view matching misjudges light sky tints by about a value step; lay a dab trial on the spot.
6. Hypothesis: broken horizontal light/dark marks on a twilight plain read as water.
7. No cast shadows in afterglow light: they read as logs or stilts.
8. Muzzle flash recipe: smoke body (graded white+orange -> mauve gray, filbert, blend), let it set about 4-9 days, then blotted white core (filbert, lay 6), then tongues of orange/red/yellow starting outside the core, then sparks spattered with medium .5.
9. work() with clip but not subtracting earlier shapes will cover them (I lost the crosses once): keep a fig_all protection mask current.

**Boot Hill, Last Light**

The scene is a graveyard on the plain just after sunset. A cowboy in a long red-brown duster stands on the left, arm straight out, and his revolver goes off in a white-hot core with orange and vermilion flames, a puff of smoke and flying sparks. Across the leaning grave crosses, a hunched zombie in rags has been clawing toward him and is caught mid-lurch. Its jaw hangs open and a dark burst of gore sprays from the back of its skull. The sky runs from deep blue-violet streaked with cloud down to a gold afterglow behind the mesas. Both figures stand dark against it, lit only by thin rims of light from the glow and the muzzle flash. I signed it bottom right.

**Still unresolved**
- **Ground:** the plain is deliberately smooth. Every textured version I tried looked like water.
- **Coat:** it could take a few more fold accents.
- **Smoke:** the gun smoke is a stylised puff.
- **Gore:** the burst reads as a red rosette with a spray around it.

**Lessons (full conditions are in the journal)**
- **Light over wet dark:** small light accents laid into open dark paint disappear, which happened four times. Let the dark set first.
- **Blending light passages:** running the blender over a figure after a light passage spreads the light across all of it, which happened three times. For rim light, a single pointed line along the traced edge with no blending worked.
- **Darkening glaze:** a transparent dark with medium 0.75–0.8, coverage 2 with gaps filled, then blended inside the same mask, darkens evenly. Without the blend it went blotchy, and with thinner it went grainy.
- **Lifting:** a rag soaked in spirits, pressed hard and refolded for three or more passes, lifts a wet glaze but leaves an outline ghost to paint over later. The knife barely lifts a thin glaze.
- **Matching colours:** holding a mix up to the canvas misjudged light sky tints by about one value step. A small dab on the spot was more reliable.
- **Shadows:** cast shadows in afterglow read as logs or stilts, so I lifted them.
- **Hypothesis:** broken horizontal light and dark marks on a twilight plain read as water.

sm_in = pile{{"lead white", 2}, {"orange chrome", 0.6}, {"cadmium yellow", 0.3}, name="sm_in"}
s2_rose = pile{{"lead white", 2}, {"vermilion", 0.35}, {"rose madder", 0.3}, {"raw umber", 0.12}, {"Naples yellow", 0.3}, name="s2_rose"}
function smoke_body(cx, cy, s, seed, clipm)
  math.randomseed(seed)
  local m = ellipse(cx + 22*s, cy - 2*s, 26*s, 18*s)
  for i = 1, 9 do
    local t = rand(0, 1)
    m = m + ellipse(cx + (20 + 75*t)*s + rand(-8,8)*s, cy - (4 + 30*t)*s + rand(-10,10)*s, (13 + 12*t)*s, (10 + 9*t)*s)
  end
  m = m:roughen(4*s, 18*s, seed):soften(2*s)
  if clipm then m = m * clipm end
  local function d(x, y) return math.sqrt(((x-cx-14*s)/1.3)^2 + (y-cy)^2) end
  work(m, {hand="body", tool={kind="filbert", width=8*s, stiffness=0.35},
    piles={{sm_in,  function(x,y) return 1 - smoothstep(14*s, 34*s, d(x,y)) end},
           {sm_mid, function(x,y) local v = d(x,y) return smoothstep(14*s, 34*s, v) * (1 - smoothstep(40*s, 70*s, v)) end},
           {sm_out, function(x,y) return smoothstep(40*s, 70*s, d(x,y)) end}},
    coverage=2.2, fill=true, angle=function(x,y) return math.atan(y-cy, x-cx) + 1.57 end, curve={0.4, 0.2}, edge="soft", clip=clipm, seed=seed})
  blend(m:shrink(2*s), {angle=-0.3})
  return m
end

## Sitting 2 (day 149-171): trials, repairs, and a judgement on each unresolved passage
New find on the fresh look: the cowboy's FACE was a flat orange-brown blob under the hat, with no ear or hair. That was the weakest passage, so I took it first.

Dark hair mask (hair_p umber/black/sienna/ultra) at the back of the head. Ear ellipse in fc_half. Pointed round 2 strokes: hair flicks past the nape, eye notch, moustache. Waited 8 days (the hand works were TACKY, the thick parts dry). Then fc_lt2/fc_hot pointed round 2.4 profile lines and an ear rim. Read as a squinting gunfighter in profile. Repeated on the painting with the same waits: it works. Lesson 1 confirmed a 5th time (the lights went on over SET paint and stayed crisp).
- Coat stain: a pale spot near (278,588), left over from the old band repair. I covered it with coat_fix, detail round 2, over dry paint, and it vanished.
- GORE (was "red rosette + spray"): IMPROVED. Scratch trial A: 11 pointed streaks radiating from the clot read as spines or horns again (the 2nd time; never do radiating streaks). Trial B, which WORKED: a cone mask from the clot along angle -0.33, half-angle .22-.34, fading out by r=62 and roughened, stippled with gore_m (medium .5) width 1.6, coverage falling from 1.6, cluster .5, feather 1. Then 2 low-force spatters (force .2-.25, spread .2) along the same line, then 2 tapered ribbon "tails" from the clot stippled with gore_dk. Result: a directional jet with a mist out of the back of the skull. On the painting it went over the dry old gore and reads as the head blown out.
- COAT folds: IMPROVED. Scratch over dry coat + coat_glaze4 (15 days): light ridge strokes (fold_lt) were too orange and stripy; ridges mixed with coat_md (fold_lt2) and then blended stayed stripy. What worked: DARK valley strokes only. fold_dk (black .5/umber .6/ultra .5/sienna .5, medium .55), filbert 9, pressure 0 -> .75 toward the hem troughs, clipped. Then a blend ribbon about 2x the stroke width along each valley, which turns it into a soft shadow. On the painting: 3 valleys over the hem troughs, x≈141, 185, 238. The skirt now hangs in folds. Hypothesis: blend() is safe when the new wet paint is DARKER than its surroundings; it is the light passages that spread (see lesson 2).
- Open grave: it was a flat black lens. I re-cut it as a slot (zg_pit) with a far inner wall in pit_wall (gm_dk .45/cw_dark .55) and ragged ends in ground colour. - SMOKE puff: ACCEPTED. Two scratch trials over dry sky: lose() with a veil (medium .55) dragged the edge into spiky streaks; an edge veil plus a rim blend fuzzed the edge but the puff stayed a puff. ## Handoff — end of sitting 2 (day 171)
State: finished, signed and all dry. "Boot Hill, Last Light".
Reflection: my heart is happy with it. The duel reads at a glance, and the warm flash and gold afterglow sit between two dark figures. This sitting gave the cowboy a face, gave the zombie's head shot a direction and gave the coat weight, and those were the three things that still bothered me. What remains stylised (puff, flat plain) belongs to the picture's poster idiom.
If taken further: (a) the zombie's arms could take one flash-lit edge on the lower forearm; (b) the hat crown highlight is a bit thick and white; (c) the pit is small and could take a few earth crumbs at its lip.
Practical lessons carried forward (hypotheses marked):
1. Light accents on dark need SET paint under them (5x). Wait until tacky or dry.
2. blend() after a LIGHT passage on a dark figure spreads it (3x). Hypothesis (1x): blending a DARK valley stroke with a ribbon about 2x its width is safe and softens it into shadow.
3. Rag lift (dip 1.0, pressure 1, refold, 3+ passes) clears a thin wet glaze but leaves an outline ghost.
4. Darkening glaze: transparent darks + medium .75-.8, hand=glaze, cov 2, fill, then blend in the same mask.
5. Hold-view matching misjudges light sky tints by about a value step; lay a dab.
6. Hypothesis: broken horizontal texture on a twilight plain reads as water.
7. No cast shadows in afterglow.
8. Flash recipe: smoke body -> set 4-9 days -> blotted white core -> tongues starting outside the core -> sparks.
9. Keep fig_all current when using clip.
10. NEW: radiating pointed streaks read as spines or horns (2x). A splash is a stippled cone of mist plus low-force spatter along one line.
11. NEW: the inside of a hole must be darker than the ground around it, or it reads as a raised slab (1x).

**Boot Hill, Last Light**

A gunfighter in a long red-brown duster fires across a graveyard just after sunset. His revolver goes off in a white-hot core with orange tongues of flame and a puff of smoke. Across the leaning grave crosses, a hunched zombie in rags, reaching for him with clawed hands, is caught mid-lurch. Blood sprays in a jet from the back of its skull. Behind them the sky runs from blue-violet cloud down to a gold afterglow over the mesas, and both figures stand dark against it.

**This sitting**
- **Cowboy's face:** it was a flat orange blob under the hat. It is now a squinting profile with an ear, hair and a moustache. I laid the lit edges only once the darks had set.
- **Gore:** it now reads as a mist with spatter thrown along one line, so the head looks shot through. A trial with pointed streaks fanning out from the wound read as horns again.
- **Coat:** three soft dark folds now run down into the hem's dips, so the skirt has weight. Laying light ridges on the folds just made stripes; the dark valleys alone worked.
- **Zombie's grave:** it was a black lens. It is now a slot with a far wall darker than the ground. My first try made the wall lighter than the ground, and it looked like a raised slab.

**Left as they are, on purpose:** the smoke puff and the smooth plain. Two smoke trials were no better than what's there, and both fit the picture's poster-like style. The tiny mark on the horizon reads as a distant headstone. The pale patch beside the zombie's face reads as light from the flash.

My heart is happy with it. If I came back, I'd add a flash-lit edge on the zombie's forearms and tone down the hat's highlight. The journal handoff has these and the updated lessons.

## Sitting 3 (day 171-181): the three "if taken further" items, each judged
Fresh look: the picture still reads at a glance (duel, flash, afterglow). Nothing new turned up as a weak passage. I worked through the three handoff items, all on DRY paint (checked with drying() first).
- (a) ZOMBIE HANDS: IMPROVED. The forearms already had a flash-lit orange rim, but it stopped at the wrists, so the clawed hands looked dead-flat. I scanned zb_keep for the top edge of each hand, then laid one pointed round 1.8 line of zb_flash over dry paint along each knuckle ridge (load .6, pressure .15 -> .6 -> .1). No blender. The rim now runs on from the arm over the back of each hand, and the hands sit in the same light as the arms. Lesson 1/2 held again: a single line over set paint, no blend.
- (b) HAT CROWN HIGHLIGHT: IMPROVED. The hat_rim lines on the crown's left edge and the brim were too pale and white-blue for a black felt hat with the glow BEHIND it. I mixed hat_sheen (cw_dark .6 / hat_rim .4) and laid it over dry paint with round 4, point .6, load .6-.65 along the same two paths. It covered the old line and left a dim cool sheen that still separates the crown from the sky. One stroke each, opaque enough to cover in one pass.
- (c) PIT / HEAP: IMPROVED. The zombie's grave heap was a pale, flat smudge at about the ground's value, with almost no edge, and it hardly read. Dab trials on the painting beside it (round 4 touches over the dry ground) showed gm_dk barely darker than the ground, heap_dk (gm_dk .65 / cw_dark .35) a clear step darker, and pit_wall darker again. I redrew the heap as a bigger rounded mound, zg_heap2 (≈886-986 x 581-627, roughened 2/5), graded with gm_dk at the top to heap_dk at the base, detail round 2.5, coverage 3.2. It now reads as a pile of thrown-out earth beside the slot, and is darker at the base, where it meets the ground. Six clod touches (heap_dk, round 2.2) at the pit's near lip almost vanished at 1x, which is harmless.
- Still ACCEPTED as before: smoke puff (poster idiom), smooth plain (water hypothesis), horizon headstone mark, pale halo by the zombie's face. A faint lighter patch of ground just left of the zombie's front foot (~790,606, old lens patch) is barely visible. Accepted: it reads as ground.
Uncertain: the clods' value. They were laid at heap_dk on mid-ground and should have shown. They may have been too small (width 2.2 at pressure .5, about 1.5u) to read at 1x, which says nothing about the colour.

## Handoff — end of sitting 3 (day 181)
State: finished, signed, all dry. "Boot Hill, Last Light".
Reflection: my heart is happy with it. This sitting was small and quiet: three finishing touches on dry paint, each a single stroke or a small mask, and I checked each in a crop and against the whole. The zombie's hands now catch the flash like its arms do. The hat is a black hat again, not a shiny one. The grave beside the zombie now has its heap, so the slot reads as dug. Nothing on the list still bothers me. What remains stylised (puff, flat plain, gore spray) belongs to the poster idiom I chose and is accepted.
If ever taken further: nothing pressing. Perhaps a slightly larger set of clods (round 3, pressure .7) at the pit lip.
Practical lessons carried forward (hypotheses marked):
1. Light accents on dark need SET paint under them (6x now). Check drying() first.
2. blend() after a LIGHT passage on a dark figure spreads it (3x). For rim light, use one pointed round line along a scanned mask edge, with no blender (worked again on the zombie knuckles). Hypothesis (1x): blending a DARK valley stroke inside a ribbon about 2x its width is safe.
3. Rag lift (dip 1.0, pressure 1, refold, 3+ passes) clears a thin wet glaze but leaves an outline ghost.
4. Darkening glaze: transparent darks + medium .75-.8, hand=glaze, cov 2, fill, then blend in the same mask.
5. Hold-view matching misjudges light sky tints by about a value step. Dab trials laid on the spot over the dry ground ARE reliable for darks too (used this sitting for the heap value).
6. Hypothesis: broken horizontal texture on a twilight plain reads as water.
7. No cast shadows in afterglow.
8. Flash recipe: smoke body -> set 4-9 days -> blotted white core -> tongues starting outside the core -> sparks.
9. Keep fig_all current when using clip (zg_heap2 added this sitting).
10. Radiating pointed streaks read as spines or horns (2x). A splash is a stippled cone of mist plus low-force spatter along one line.
11. The inside of a hole must be darker than the ground (1x). Hypothesis (1x): a mound needs a value step darker than the ground at its base to read at all on a dark plain.
12. A highlight that is too bright on a dark object can be knocked back with a single stroke of a mix of the dark and the highlight (about 60/40) over dry paint. It covers in one pass (1x).
I've reviewed everything, so I'm ready to give my final reply now.

**Boot Hill, Last Light**

A gunfighter in a long red-brown duster fires across a graveyard just after sunset. His revolver goes off in a white-hot core with orange tongues of flame and a puff of smoke. Across the leaning grave crosses, a hunched zombie in rags reaches for him with clawed hands, caught mid-lurch as blood sprays from the back of its skull. Behind them the sky runs from blue-violet cloud down to a gold afterglow over the mesas. Both figures stand dark against it.

**This sitting**

This was a short, quiet sitting. I made the three changes I'd listed last time, all over paint that had already dried:
- **Zombie's hands:** the orange glow from the gunshot lit its arms but stopped at the wrists, so the hands looked flat. One thin orange line along each set of knuckles now carries that light onto the hands.
- **Hat:** the highlight on the crown and brim was too pale and shiny for a black felt hat with the glow behind it. A single stroke of the hat's dark mixed with that highlight colour turned it into a dim sheen that still separates the hat from the sky.
- **Zombie's grave:** the heap beside the open grave was about the same value as the ground and barely showed. I tested a few small dabs of colour next to it first. Then I repainted it as a larger rounded mound that darkens toward its base, so the open grave now reads as freshly dug. The few small clods I added at the edge of the hole are too small to see at full view, which does no harm.

**Left as they are, on purpose:** the smoke puff, the smooth plain, the stylised blood spray, the tiny headstone on the horizon and the pale patch beside the zombie's face. They suit the picture's poster-like style.

My heart is happy with it, and nothing on my list still bothers me. The journal has notes on each change and an updated handoff with the practical lessons. Two lessons are new: a heap needs to be darker than the ground at its base to show up, and an over-bright highlight can be toned down with one stroke of the object's dark mixed with that highlight.

## Handoff — end of sitting 4 (day 191)
State: finished, signed, all dry. "Boot Hill, Last Light".
Reflection: my heart is happy with it. This sitting added one small thing I wanted for the fun of it: spurs, so that the gunfighter is a cowboy down to his heels. I trialled them on scratch first, over the same dry substrate, and the first version (a long bright band) was wrong in a useful way. Nothing else calls for work. The stylised passages (puff, flat plain, gore jet) belong to the poster idiom.
If ever taken further: nothing pressing. A bit of brass on the gun's cylinder could catch the flash, but the gun is a dark shape against the halo and reads well as it is.
Practical lessons carried forward (hypotheses marked):
1. Light accents on dark need SET paint under them (7x). Check drying() first.
2. blend() after a LIGHT passage on a dark figure spreads it (3x). For rim light use one pointed round line along a scanned mask edge, and no blender. Hypothesis (1x): blending a DARK valley stroke in a ribbon about 2x its width is safe.
3. Rag lift (dip 1.0, pressure 1, refold, 3+ passes) clears a thin wet glaze but leaves an outline ghost.
4. Darkening glaze: transparent darks + medium .75-.8, hand=glaze, cov 2, fill, then blend in the same mask.
5. Hold-view matching misjudges light sky tints by about a value step. Dab trials on the spot are reliable.
6. Hypothesis: broken horizontal texture on a twilight plain reads as water.
7. No cast shadows in afterglow.
8. Flash recipe: smoke body -> set 4-9 days -> blotted white core -> tongues starting outside the core -> sparks.
9. Keep fig_all current when using clip.
10. Radiating pointed streaks read as spines or horns at splash scale (2x). At about 4u (a spur rowel) they read as a star, which is fine there (1x).
11. The inside of a hole must be darker than the ground (1x). A mound needs a darker base to read (1x).
12. Knock back an over-bright highlight on a dark object with one stroke of a mix of the dark and the highlight (about 60/40) over dry paint (1x). The same mixing idea gave the spur band (spur_m .55 / cw_dark .45) and the boot sheen (cw_dark .6 / rim_warm .4): a metal or leather accent on a dark object in twilight should be the dark tinted toward the light, not the light itself (2x).
13. Trials on the scratch canvas: lay the same ground and figure paint and dry them as long as on the painting. It took about 14-17 days for cw_dark round-2.5 detail at cov 3.2 to go fully dry.

**Boot Hill, Last Light**

A gunfighter in a long red-brown coat fires across a graveyard just after sunset. His revolver goes off in a white-hot core with orange tongues of flame and a puff of smoke. Across the leaning grave crosses, a hunched zombie in rags reaches for him with clawed hands, and blood sprays out of the back of its skull. Behind them the sky runs from blue-violet cloud down to a gold afterglow over the mesas, with both figures dark against it.

**This sitting**

I made one change, mostly for the pleasure of it: **spurs**. His boots were plain black shapes that could have been anyone's shoes, and I wanted him to be a cowboy right down to his heels.

- **Trial:** I tried them on the scratch canvas first, over the same ground and boot paint, dried for about the same 14–17 days as on the painting.

- **What worked:** a short band mixed from the spur colour and the boot's black, a little six-spiked rowel, one warm glint on the rowel and a faint warm sheen on each toe.
- **On the painting:** I laid that version on both boots over dry paint without blending. Close up they look like spurs, and at full view they're two tiny glints that don't compete with the gunshot.

**Left as they are, on purpose:** I looked again at each passage I'd marked unresolved, in close-up. The cartoon smoke puff, the smooth plain, the blood spray, the hat, the grave and its heap, and the small leftover marks all suit the picture's poster-like style. I also found a tiny dark speck in the plain that's invisible at full view, so I left it.

My heart is happy with it. The journal has a note on the spur trial and an updated handoff with the practical lessons. One is new: on a dark object in twilight, a metal or leather highlight works better as the dark mixed toward the light colour than as the light colour itself. Nothing is pressing. If I ever come back, a touch of brass on the gun's cylinder might catch the muzzle flash, but the gun already shows up well as a dark shape against the glow.

## Handoff, end of sitting 5 (day 217)
State: finished, signed, and all dry (I waited 14 days and checked). Title: "Boot Hill, Last Light".
Reflection: my heart is happy with it. This sitting fixed two things a fresh look turned up. The open grave had read as a slab, and now it's a dark slot. The gun hand had read as a ball, and now it's a fist on a grip. I tried the hand on scratch first, and the first version failed in a useful way (a round butt reads as a ball). In the gallery view the duel reads at once: the white-hot muzzle, the head shot, two dark figures against the afterglow. The stylised passages belong to the poster idiom and are accepted.
If ever taken further: nothing pressing. The zombie's feet are plain mitten shapes. They could take a torn sole or a toe, but I'd keep them dark.
Practical lessons carried forward (hypotheses marked):
1. Light accents on dark need SET paint under them (8x). Check drying() first; 12-14 days covers round-2.x detail work.
2. blend() after a LIGHT passage on a dark figure spreads it (3x). For rim light, use one pointed round line along a scanned mask edge, with no blender. Hypothesis (1x): blending a DARK valley stroke in a ribbon about 2x its width is safe.
3. Rag lift (dip 1.0, pressure 1, refold, 3+ passes) clears a thin wet glaze but leaves an outline ghost.
4. Darkening glaze: transparent darks + medium .75-.8, hand=glaze, cov 2, fill, then blend in the same mask.
5. Hold-view matching misjudges light sky tints by about a value step. Dab trials on the spot are reliable (also for the pit dark this sitting).
6. Hypothesis: broken horizontal texture on a twilight plain reads as water.
7. No cast shadows in afterglow.
8. Flash recipe: smoke body -> set 4-9 days -> blotted white core -> tongues starting outside the core -> sparks.
9. Keep fig_all current when using clip (cb_hand3 and cb_butt added).
10. Radiating pointed streaks read as spines or horns at splash scale (2x), but as a star at about 4u (1x).
11. The inside of a hole must be darker than the ground, and the far wall seen through the opening must be nearly as dark as the slot. A lighter band with a hard edge reads as the top of a box (2x). A mound needs a darker base (1x).
12. Accents on a dark object in twilight should be the dark tinted toward the light (about 55/45 to 60/40), not the light itself (3x: hat, spurs, grip strap).
13. Scratch trials: copy the painting's ground and passage at the same coordinates (a replica function with an offset makes several side by side) and dry them as long as on the painting.
14. Hypothesis (1x): for small objects, shape carries the read more than the lights do. Rounded = ball, angular corners = made thing.

**Boot Hill, Last Light**

A gunfighter in a long red-brown coat fires across a graveyard just after sunset. The revolver goes off in a white-hot core with tongues of orange flame. Across the leaning crosses, a hunched zombie with clawed hands reaches for him as blood sprays from the back of its skull. Behind them the blue-violet cloud runs down to a gold afterglow over the mesas, and both figures stand dark against it.

**This sitting**

A fresh look turned up two passages that read as the wrong thing, and I fixed both:

- **The open grave read as a raised slab.** Its far inner wall had been a pale band with a hard edge, so it looked like the top of a box. I laid a small dark trial on the spot first, then repainted the wall nearly as dark as the slot. It now reads as a hole cut into the ground beside its heap. I also painted over a faint grey blob by the zombie's front foot with the ground colours.
- **The gun hand was a ball on a stick.** I tried this on the scratch canvas first, on copies of the passage dried as long as on the painting. My first try, adding a rounded grip below the fist, read as a dangling ball. The version that worked had three parts:
  - a squarer fist, with a flat thumb line on top and a heel at the back
  - an angular grip flaring back below the heel, and a trigger-guard loop
  - after 12 days' drying, four separate flash-lit knuckle strokes down the front of the fist
  
  On the painting it now reads as a fist gripping a revolver, even at full view.

**Left as they are, on purpose:** I checked each passage I'd marked unresolved in a close crop. The cartoon smoke puff, the smooth plain, the blood spray, the distant headstone mark and the small pale fleck on the hatband (it looks like a concho) all suit the picture's bold, poster-like style. The zombie's plain dark feet read as worn shoes, and adding detail there would pull the eye down from the head shot.

My heart is happy with it. Everything is dry, and the journal has an updated handoff with the practical lessons. Two are new or sharpened:
- **Holes:** the inside of a hole has to be nearly as dark as the opening. A lighter band with a hard edge reads as a box.
- **Small objects (seen once, so still a guess):** the shape does more than the highlights. Rounded shapes read as balls, while angular corners read as made things like a grip or a fist.

local function prof(m, x0, x1, y0, y1, step)
  local out = {}
  for y = y0, y1, step or 3 do
    local xl, xr
    for x = x0, x1 do if m:at(x,y) > 0.5 then xl = x break end end
    for x = x1, x0, -1 do if m:at(x,y) > 0.5 then xr = x break end end
    out[#out+1] = y .. ":" .. tostring(xl) .. "-" .. tostring(xr)
  end
  return table.concat(out, " ")
end

events.text:
## Handoff, end of sitting 6 (day 245)
State: finished, signed, and all dry (I waited 14 days and checked). Title: "Boot Hill, Last Light".
Reflection: my heart is happy with it. This was a short sitting about one thing, the zombie's feet. They were the last passage that still looked like a placeholder. They now read as shoes mid-stride, with the back foot pushing off toward the cowboy, so the lurch carries all the way down the figure. In the gallery view the duel reads at once: the white-hot muzzle, the head shot, and two dark figures against the afterglow. The stylised passages (the puff, the flat plain, the gore jet) belong to the poster idiom, and I accept them.
If ever taken further: nothing pressing. I'd leave it.
Practical lessons carried forward (hypotheses marked):
1. Light accents on dark need SET paint under them (9x). Check drying() first; 12-14 days covers round-2.x detail work.
2. blend() after a LIGHT passage on a dark figure spreads it (3x). For rim light, use one pointed round line along a scanned mask edge, with no blender. Hypothesis (1x): blending a DARK valley stroke in a ribbon about 2x its width is safe.
3. Rag lift (dip 1.0, pressure 1, refold, 3+ passes) clears a thin wet glaze but leaves an outline ghost.
4. Darkening glaze: transparent darks + medium .75-.8, hand=glaze, cov 2, fill, then blend in the same mask.
5. Hold-view matching misjudges light sky tints by about a value step. Dab trials on the spot are reliable.
6. Hypothesis: broken horizontal texture on a twilight plain reads as water.
7. No cast shadows in afterglow.
8. Flash recipe: smoke body -> set 4-9 days -> blotted white core -> tongues starting outside the core -> sparks.
9. Keep fig_all current when using clip (zb_feet3 added).
10. Radiating pointed streaks read as spines or horns at splash scale (2x), but as a star at about 4u (1x).
11. The inside of a hole must be darker than the ground, and the far wall seen through it nearly as dark as the slot (2x). A mound needs a darker base (1x).
12. Accents on a dark object in twilight should be the dark tinted toward the light, about 60/40 (4x: hat, spurs, grip strap, zombie toe-caps).
13. Scratch trials: copy the painting's ground and passage at the same coordinates (a replica function with an offset) and dry them as long as on the painting.
14. For small objects, shape carries the read more than the lights do (2x: gun hand, zombie feet). Rounded blobs read as balls or lumps; angular corners (heel, flat sole, a straight edge) read as made things.
15. When reshaping a dark object over a two-part background (ground + pit), cover the excess with each background's own paint, split by the background's mask (1x, it worked cleanly).

I've finished the painting, **Boot Hill, Last Light**.

A gunfighter in a long red-brown coat fires across a graveyard just after sunset. His revolver goes off in a white-hot core with orange tongues of flame. Across the leaning crosses, a hunched zombie with clawed hands reaches for him as blood sprays from the back of its skull. The blue-violet cloud runs down to a gold afterglow over the mesas, and both figures stand dark against it.

**This sitting:** I had one thing left over from last time, the zombie's feet. They were plain mitten shapes, and the back one was a round lump hanging off the leg. I tried new feet on the scratch canvas first, on copies of the passage dried as long as the painting's. The first version of the back foot came out too short and stubby; a longer one worked. Then I painted it on the painting:
- **The shapes:** angular shoes with a flat sole and a squared heel. The back foot is heel-up, pushing off toward the cowboy.
- **The cleanup:** I covered the old shapes with the ground's own colours, and with the pit's dark where they overlapped the open grave.
- **The finish:** after 14 days' drying, a faint flash-lit line on each toe, and a small dark patch on the ground under each shoe.

The zombie's lurch now runs from its reaching hands all the way down to its feet. I also painted out a tiny pale fleck on the hat.

**Left as they are, on purpose:** I checked each of these again in a close crop. The cartoon smoke puff, the smooth plain, the blood spray and the distant headstone mark all suit the picture's bold, poster-like style.

My heart is happy with it, and I'd leave it here. Everything is dry, and the journal has an updated handoff with the practical lessons. Two lessons got stronger this sitting:
- **Small objects:** shape carries them more than highlights do. A rounded blob reads as a lump; angular corners read as a made thing. This has now held twice, for the gun hand and the feet.
- **Accents on dark objects:** a highlight on a dark object in twilight works best as the dark tinted toward the light, not the light colour itself. This has now held four times.

events.text:
## Handoff, end of sitting 7 (painting at day 245; nothing new laid)
State: finished, signed, all dry. "Boot Hill, Last Light".
Reflection: my heart is happy with it. This sitting was a look-and-test sitting. The one thing that nagged me in a crop, the open grave reading a bit like a plank, got six honest scratch trials over replicas dried as long as the painting's. Each variant pointed somewhere worse: bevel, teeth, box lid, log, blade. That tells me the plain dark slit is already the least object-like way to say "hole" at this size in this idiom, and beside its heap it does say it. So I left the painting untouched, on purpose. In the gallery view the duel reads at once: the white-hot muzzle, the head shot, two dark figures against the gold afterglow, the crosses on the plain.
If ever taken further: nothing pressing. I'd leave it.
Practical lessons carried forward (hypotheses marked):
1. Light accents on dark need SET paint under them (9x). Check drying() first; 12-14 days covers round-2.x detail work.
2. blend() after a LIGHT passage on a dark figure spreads it (3x). For rim light, use one pointed round line along a scanned mask edge, with no blender. Hypothesis (1x): blending a DARK valley stroke in a ribbon about 2x its width is safe.
3. Rag lift (dip 1.0, pressure 1, refold, 3+ passes) clears a thin wet glaze but leaves an outline ghost.
4. Darkening glaze: transparent darks + medium .75-.8, hand=glaze, cov 2, fill, then blend in the same mask.
5. Hold-view matching misjudges light sky tints by about a value step. Dab trials on the spot are reliable.
6. Hypothesis: broken horizontal texture on a twilight plain reads as water.
7. No cast shadows in afterglow.
8. Flash recipe: smoke body -> set 4-9 days -> blotted white core -> tongues starting outside the core -> sparks.
9. Keep fig_all current when using clip.
10. Radiating pointed streaks read as spines or horns at splash scale (2x), but as a star at about 4u (1x).
11. A hole: its inside must be darker than the ground, and the far wall nearly as dark as the slot. Any lighter band with an edge inside a dark slot reads as a box top or bevel (3x now). A mound needs a darker base (1x).
12. Accents on a dark object in twilight should be the dark tinted toward the light, about 60/40 (4x).
13. Scratch trials: copy the painting's ground and passage at the same coordinates (a replica function with an offset) and dry them as long as on the painting. A third replica kept untouched is a useful comparator.
14. For small objects, shape carries the read more than the lights do (2x). Rounded blobs read as lumps; angular corners read as made things.
15. When reshaping a dark object over a two-part background, cover the excess with each background's own paint, split by its mask (1x).
16. NEW hypothesis (1x): a vertical light-to-dark gradient across a horizontal dark bar reads as a cylinder (a log). Tiny light tops on lip clods read as teeth.
17. NEW (1x): ground piles (flat 4, cov 3.5) over a dry dark slot cover it cleanly in one pass. Removal is a real option for a small dark shape.
18. When several variants of a repair each read worse in different ways, the original is probably the right simplification for the idiom. Accepting it is a decision, not a give-up.
I'm ready to finalize my response now.

The painting is still **Boot Hill, Last Light**, and I didn't add a single stroke to it this sitting. All the work happened on the scratch canvas.

A gunfighter in a long red-brown coat fires across a graveyard just after sunset. His revolver goes off in a white-hot core with orange tongues of flame. Across the leaning crosses, a hunched zombie lurches toward him on clawed hands and worn shoes, and blood sprays from the back of its skull. Behind them the blue-violet cloud runs down into a gold afterglow over the mesas, and both figures stand dark against it.

**This sitting:** I looked at the whole picture fresh and in close crops. One thing nagged me: in a crop, the open grave behind the zombie's feet looked a little like a dark plank lying on the ground. I copied that part of the painting onto the scratch canvas, dried as long as the original, and tried six fixes. Every one read as something else:
- **A lighter end wall:** looked like a bevelled edge.

Actually, maybe better to tear open the existing heap itself rather than add a separate slot — a ragged dark cavity torn into its top-left near the cross, with the mound's silhouette continuing as a rim behind the hole. Since the heap already has a rounded profile rather than a flat-bottomed slab like in T1, the crater there should read more like a burrow or torn opening than a geometric slot, though I worry it could also just look like a horizontal dark smear near the top.

local function bbox(m, x0, y0, x1, y1)
  local a, b, c, d = 1e9, 1e9, -1e9, -1e9
  for y = y0, y1, 0.5 do for x = x0, x1, 0.5 do
    if m:at(x, y) > 0.5 then a = math.min(a, x); b = math.min(b, y); c = math.max(c, x); d = math.max(d, y) end
  end end
  return string.format("%.1f %.1f %.1f %.1f", a, b, c, d)
end

## Sitting 8 (day 245-273): the open grave, re-thought instead of repaired
Fresh look (whole, survey, value/squint, gallery, crops of zombie, head/gun, puff, pit). The picture reads at a glance as before. The one thing that still bothered me was the PLANK again: a dark rectangle lying flat on the ground beside a separate heap. Last sitting I tried six shapes for the HOLE, and each read as a different object. So this time I questioned the arrangement itself (lesson 18 said to reconsider the composition or method if a repair keeps recreating the problem): why is the hole next to the heap at all? A zombie that clawed its way out leaves a BROKEN MOUND, not a dug trench.
- SCRATCH 1 (fresh, replicas at dx 0/-300, land body + slot + heap + cross + legs/shoes, dried 16 days):
  T1: slot removed, a broken mound with a dark crater and clods. The mound was too wide and flat and read as a second heap. FAIL.
  T2: a spoil bank behind the slot. It read as a dark slab again. FAIL.
- SCRATCH 2 (fresh, 3 replicas at dx 0/-300/-600, dried 16 days):
  R (-300): removal only (pz ground piles, flat 4 detail, cov 3.5, clip, over dry). Clean. The heap then reads as a grave mound under its cross.
  V1 (0): removal + a smooth elliptical crater (cw_dark) in the heap's top. It read as a black lens/disc, too neat (lesson 14: round = object).
  V2 (-300): + lumps standing above the crater lip (gm_dk ellipses). They read as a row of grey pebbles. FAIL; the lumps were too regular and too light.
  V3 (0, over dry heap paint): a TORN crater, an irregular zigzag poly (~915-954 x 586-596, roughen 1.1/2.2), cw_dark, round 1.6 detail, cov 3.5. It reads as a ragged dark opening broken through the mound top. GOOD.
  V4 (-600): V3 + 5 small heap_dk clods (round 1.6, ellipses r 1.6-2.8) trailing from the mound toward the zombie's back foot. Reads as earth kicked out. GOOD.
- PAINTING: I did a dab trial first (the left 22u of the slot covered with pz ground piles over dry; it vanished cleanly), then the rest of the slot outside the heap with pz and the slice inside the heap with the heap piles (gm_dk->heap_dk by y, round 2.5, cov 3.5). Dried 14 days. Then V4 (crater cr_heap + clods cl_heap), all over dry paint. Both were added to fig_all. Dried 14 more days.
  RESULT: at full view and in the gallery the grave is now a mound under the leaning cross, burst open at the top, with clods trailing to the zombie's heel. The story is simpler: it climbed out of THAT grave. In the value view there is a very faint lighter band where the slot was (~795-890, y 588-603). It is invisible in colour at 1x, and in a crop it reads as an unevenness in the ground. ACCEPT.

events.text:
## Handoff, end of sitting 8 (day 273)
State: finished, signed, all dry (waited 14 days after the last touch and checked). "Boot Hill, Last Light".
Reflection: my heart is happy with it, and happier than last time. The open grave had nagged me for two sittings. Last sitting I accepted it after six failed shapes. This sitting I stopped repairing the hole and asked whether a separate trench belonged there at all. It didn't. A zombie doesn't dig a neat slot; it bursts up through its own mound. With the slot gone, the zombie's grave is now the same kind of mound as the others on the hill, only torn open at the top, with a few clods trailing to its heel. The story reads more simply, and nothing in the lower right looks like a plank any more. In the gallery view the duel reads at once: the white-hot muzzle, the head shot, two dark figures against the gold afterglow, and the crosses on the plain.
If ever taken further: nothing pressing. I'd leave it.
Uncertain: the faint lighter band where the slot was shows only in the value view. If the overpaint's slight tone difference ever shows in colour (it doesn't at 1x now), one more pz pass over dry paint would settle it.
Practical lessons carried forward (hypotheses marked):
1. Light accents on dark need SET paint under them (9x). Check drying() first; 12-14 days covers round-2.x detail work.
2. blend() after a LIGHT passage on a dark figure spreads it (3x). For rim light, use one pointed round line along a scanned mask edge, with no blender. Hypothesis (1x): blending a DARK valley stroke in a ribbon about 2x its width is safe.
3. Rag lift (dip 1.0, pressure 1, refold, 3+ passes) clears a thin wet glaze but leaves an outline ghost.
4. Darkening glaze: transparent darks + medium .75-.8, hand=glaze, cov 2, fill, then blend in the same mask.
5. Hold-view matching misjudges light sky tints by about a value step. Dab trials on the spot are reliable.
6. Hypothesis: broken horizontal texture on a twilight plain reads as water.
7. No cast shadows in afterglow.
8. Flash recipe: smoke body -> set 4-9 days -> blotted white core -> tongues starting outside the core -> sparks.
9. Keep fig_all current when using clip (cr_heap, cl_heap added).
10. Radiating pointed streaks read as spines or horns at splash scale (2x), but as a star at about 4u (1x).
11. A hole inside a dark slot: any lighter band with an edge reads as a box top or bevel (3x). A mound needs a darker base (1x).
12. Accents on a dark object in twilight should be the dark tinted toward the light, about 60/40 (4x).
13. Scratch trials: copy the painting's ground and passage at the same coordinates (a replica function with an offset, 3 side by side) and dry them as long as on the painting.
14. For small objects, shape carries the read (3x). Smooth rounds and ellipses read as balls, lumps or discs; angular or jagged outlines read as made things or torn openings.
15. When reshaping a dark object over a two-part background, cover the excess with each background's own paint, split by its mask (2x: also the slot slice inside the heap this sitting).
16. Hypothesis (1x): a vertical light-to-dark gradient across a horizontal dark bar reads as a log. Tiny light tops on clods read as teeth; small DARK clods (heap_dk) read as kicked earth.
17. Ground piles (flat 4, cov 3.5) over a dry dark shape cover it cleanly in one pass (2x).
18. When several repairs of a shape each read as a different wrong object, first question whether the shape belongs there at all (the arrangement), before accepting it. Here, changing the arrangement fixed what six shape variants couldn't (1x).
I've done a final review, and I'm ready to reply.

The painting is still **Boot Hill, Last Light**. This sitting I finally fixed the open grave, the one passage that had bothered me for two sittings.

A gunfighter in a long red-brown coat fires across a graveyard just after sunset. His revolver goes off in a white-hot core with orange tongues of flame. Across the leaning crosses, a hunched zombie lurches toward him on clawed hands and worn shoes, and blood sprays from the back of its skull. Behind them the blue-violet cloud runs down into a gold afterglow over the mesas, and both figures stand dark against it.

**This sitting:** last time I tried six new shapes for the dark slot behind the zombie's feet. Each one looked like some other object (a bevel, teeth, a box lid, a log, a blade), so I left it as it was. This time I asked whether a separate trench belonged there at all. A zombie doesn't dig a neat hole; it breaks up through its own grave mound.

I tested this on the scratch canvas first, on copies of that part of the painting dried as long as the original:
- **A smooth oval crater in the mound:** looked like a black disc.
- **Lumps around its rim:** looked like pebbles.
- **What worked:** a torn, jagged opening in the top of the mound, with a few small dark clods trailing toward the zombie's heel.

On the painting I covered the slot with the ground's own colours over dry paint, waited two weeks of painting time, and then laid in the torn opening and the clods. The zombie's grave is now a mound like the others on the hill, burst open at the top. Nothing in the lower right reads as a plank any more, and the story is simpler: it climbed out of that grave.

**Left as they are, on purpose:** I checked each of these again in a close crop and wrote a judgement for each in the journal.
- **Still accepted:** the cartoon smoke puff, the gore spray, the smooth plain and the cloud streak in the upper right all suit the picture's bold, poster-like style.
- **One small uncertainty:** where the slot was, there's a very faint lighter band. It shows only in the black-and-white value view, not in colour at normal size. If it ever starts to show, one more pass of the ground colours over dry paint should cover it.

My heart is happy with it, more than at the end of last sitting. The journal has an updated handoff with the practical lessons. The new one: when every fix of a shape reads as some other object, first ask whether that shape belongs in the picture at all, before accepting it.

function cross_shape(bx, by, h, lean, barTilt)
  local w = h * 0.075
  local ux, uy = math.sin(lean), -math.cos(lean)       -- up direction
  local tx, ty = math.cos(lean + barTilt), math.sin(lean + barTilt)  -- bar direction
  local top = {bx + ux*h, by + uy*h}
  local post = ribbon({{bx, by}, {bx + ux*h*0.5, by + uy*h*0.5}, top}, {w*1.05, w, w*0.95})
  local cx, cy = bx + ux*h*0.74, by + uy*h*0.74
  local L = h * 0.29
  local bar = ribbon({{cx - tx*L, cy - ty*L}, {cx + tx*L, cy + ty*L*1.0}}, {w*0.85, w*0.9})
  return post + bar, {bx=bx, by=by, ux=ux, uy=uy, tx=tx, ty=ty, h=h, w=w, cx=cx, cy=cy, L=L}
end

events.text:
Looking at the zombie head in full scale, the small round strokes for the eye socket and mouth read clearly even at 1x, giving it a believable pale, lit profile with a dark open mouth. It's working well already, which makes me pause on whether the face needs more detail or if it's better left as is.

Stepping back, the composition holds together: the cowboy large at left, the zombie smaller at right suggesting distance, the flash between them, streaky sky at upper left, flat mauve ground, and the crosses all read as a coherent poster. The zombie's torso as an olive-brown sack-like shape with a hunched back and flaring tail works as a strong silhouette, and the cowboy's long straight arm is fine as is.

Thinking about small additions that might be fun — maybe a thin crescent moon near the sunset glow, since a young moon setting shortly after the sun is physically plausible and could add a nice touch to the sky.

But a crescent moon risks competing with the flash and gore for visual attention, so it might not be necessary. A pair of distant vulture silhouettes circling over Boot Hill feels more fitting thematically — a classic western touch that would add some depth to the sky without overwhelming the scene.

Still, my real focus should be the zombie's face itself, since that's the subject of the piece. I want to check if the face reads clearly as a zombie at thumbnail scale, and whether features like a brighter cheekbone plane, deeper eye socket, or a hanging jaw would make it more legible — so I should pull up the zombie head crop again in gallery mode to check values.

Squinting at it, the flash core with flames and the cool blue-white smoke puff beside it reads well against the zombie silhouette and cowboy. The composition feels solid after eight sittings, and now I'm weighing whether to keep pushing further or explore something else I'd enjoy.

Looking critically though: the zombie's head-shot moment reads fine as impact, the cowboy's coat is a big dull mass but acceptable, and the foreground ground between the figures is a large smooth empty mauve void that could use some sparse scrub or stones to anchor it. I recall a journal note about adding scrub silhouettes and a scrub function that was defined, but I don't see any scrub rendered in the image — it may have been painted over during the later land repaint, so I want to check the log for where scrub was used.

A fun idea occurs to me: a tumbleweed rolling between the two duelists would be a classic, witty western touch. It's essentially a tangled ball shape with rim lighting from the glow behind it, placed mid-ground around x 640, y 600 at modest size — though I worry it could pull focus from the main action or clutter the composition.

I could also place the tumbleweed higher, silhouetted against the bright horizon near the crosses, but then it'd read too small and distant to matter much. Stepping back, I should prioritize the zombie's face since it's the actual subject per the brief—cowboy blasting a zombie—while the tumbleweed is just decoration I can add afterward if there's room.

Looking at the zombie head at roughly 40px with 5-10px features, it reads as a legible ghoul at normal viewing scale, though I've never specifically stress-tested whether it's actually strong enough. Since the flash sits to the left and the zombie faces directly into it, the lit edge should be warm and bright, but right now it's just a pale yellow-green line that's underselling the lighting.

I'm weighing whether to add a light orange-gold accent to the face's front planes, similar to the warm rim already on the arms, to make the head pop as a secondary focal point alongside the gore. But the paint there is fully dry, so this would need to be a careful scratch trial rather than a blended adjustment.

Before committing, I want to replicate the head passage dry first — same skin tones and features — then test a new version with lit planes in warm flash-gold, a deeper socket with a glint, and visible teeth, comparing the two side by side. First though, I should check the state of the surrounding area and confirm everything's dry, then take a full survey at full detail across the four tiles to see if anything else needs attention before diving in.
